# 2 Samuel Chapter 15 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic)
**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Leningrad Codex (B19A), Folios 185r–186r | **Source Image:** source-texts/hebrew-OT/2SA_015_page_001.jpg, 2SA_015_page_002.jpg, 2SA_015_page_003.jpg

---

**1** After this, Absalom got himself a chariot, horses, and fifty men to run ahead of him as an escort. **2** He would get up early and position himself at the side of the road leading to the city gate. Whenever anyone came with a case to bring before the king for a ruling, Absalom would call out, "What city are you from?" When the man answered, "Your servant is from such-and-such tribe in Israel," **3** Absalom would say, "Look, your case is clearly valid and just — but the king hasn't appointed anyone to hear cases like yours."

**4** Then Absalom would add, "If only someone would make me judge over this land! Then anyone with a grievance or a dispute could come to me, and I would see that they got justice."

**5** And whenever someone approached to bow before him, Absalom would reach out, take the man's hand, and embrace him with a kiss. **6** Absalom did this with every Israelite who came to the king for a ruling. And so, bit by bit, Absalom stole the hearts of the people of Israel.

**7** At the end of four years, Absalom said to the king, "Please let me go to Hebron to fulfill a vow I made to the LORD. **8** While I was living in Geshur in Aram, I made this vow: 'If the LORD brings me back to Jerusalem, I will worship him in Hebron.'"

**9** "Go in peace," the king said. So Absalom set out for Hebron.

**10** But Absalom had already planted agents throughout the tribes of Israel with these instructions: "The moment you hear the trumpet blast, shout, 'Absalom is king in Hebron!'"

**11** Two hundred men from Jerusalem went with Absalom. They had been invited as guests and went in complete innocence, knowing nothing about the plot.

**12** While offering sacrifices, Absalom also sent for Ahithophel the Gilonite — David's own counselor — summoning him from his hometown of Giloh. The conspiracy gained momentum. The number of people joining Absalom kept growing.

**13** A messenger rushed to David with the news: "The hearts of the men of Israel have swung to Absalom."

**14** David said to his officials in Jerusalem, "We have to leave — now! If we don't move fast, none of us will escape. Absalom will overtake us, bring disaster on us, and put the city to the sword."

**15** The king's servants said, "Whatever the king decides, we're with you."

**16** The king set out on foot, his entire household with him. He left behind ten concubines to look after the palace.

**17** The king went out with all his people on foot and stopped at the last house on the edge of the city.

**18** His whole personal guard marched past him — the Cherethites, the Pelethites, and all six hundred Gittites who had followed him from Gath — filing past the king.

**19** The king said to Ittai the Gittite, "Why are you coming too? Go back and stay with the new king. You're a foreigner — an exile from your own country. **20** You only arrived yesterday! Should I drag you along on my wandering today, when I don't even know where I'm going? Go back and take your men with you. And may the LORD show you his faithful love and truth."

**21** But Ittai answered the king, "As the LORD lives, and as my lord the king lives — wherever you are, whether it means life or death, that's where I'll be."

**22** David said to Ittai, "Then come. March on." So Ittai the Gittite marched past with all his men and all their families.

**23** The whole countryside was weeping loudly as the people streamed past. The king crossed the Kidron Valley, and all the people headed toward the wilderness road.

**24** Zadok was there too, along with all the Levites, carrying the ark of the covenant of God. They set the ark down and waited until everyone had cleared the city. Abiathar was also there.

**25** Then the king said to Zadok, "Take the ark of God back to the city. If I find favor in the LORD's eyes, he will bring me back and let me see the ark and his dwelling place again. **26** But if he says, 'I take no pleasure in you' — well, here I am. Let him do with me whatever he thinks best."

**27** The king said to Zadok the priest, "Look — you and Abiathar go back to the city in peace. Take your two sons with you — your son Ahimaaz and Abiathar's son Jonathan. **28** I'll be waiting at the river crossings in the wilderness until I hear from you."

**29** So Zadok and Abiathar took the ark of God back to Jerusalem and stayed there.

**30** David made his way up the Mount of Olives, weeping as he climbed. His head was covered and his feet were bare. Everyone with him covered their heads too, and they went up weeping.

**31** Someone told David, "Ahithophel has joined the conspirators with Absalom." David prayed, "LORD, turn Ahithophel's advice into nonsense."

**32** When David reached the summit — the place where people worshiped God — there was Hushai the Archite coming to meet him, his robe ripped and dirt on his head.

**33** David said to him, "If you come with me, you'll only slow me down. **34** But if you go back to the city and tell Absalom, 'I'll serve you, O king — I served your father before, and now I'll serve you' — then you can counter Ahithophel's advice for me.

**35** Zadok and Abiathar the priests are there. Whatever you hear in the palace, pass it along to them. **36** They have their two sons there — Zadok's son Ahimaaz and Abiathar's son Jonathan. Send word to me through them — anything you learn."

**37** So Hushai, David's trusted friend, arrived in the city just as Absalom was entering Jerusalem.

---
## PNEUMA's Meaning Notes

**Verse 1 — the chariot and runners:** Absalom's self-appointment of a chariot escort is a deliberate imitation of kingship. The fifty runners are a royal bodyguard — the same kind of entourage that Adonijah will later copy (1 Kgs 1:5). Absalom is performing kingship before he claims it.

**Verse 4 — "If only someone would make me judge":** This is political theater at its most effective. Absalom positions himself not as a usurper but as a public servant being denied the chance to help. The word "judge" (*shofet*) reaches back before the monarchy itself, to the era of Judges — implying that the institution of kingship has failed the people.

**Verse 6 — "stole the hearts":** The narrator's word choice is moral commentary. He doesn't say Absalom "won" hearts or "turned" hearts — he *stole* them. The verb *ganav* is the verb of the eighth commandment. What Absalom does to Israel's loyalty is a form of theft.

**Verse 20 — "faithful love and truth":** David's parting blessing to Ittai uses *chesed ve-emet* — the great covenant pair. That David speaks these words to a Philistine soldier — a foreigner and an exile — is one of the most theologically generous moments in the entire narrative. At his lowest point, David extends God's covenant language to an outsider.

**Verse 21 — Ittai's oath:** Ittai's declaration echoes Ruth's famous vow (Ruth 1:16-17) — "wherever you go, I will go." A Philistine mercenary makes the same kind of radical commitment to David that Ruth made to Naomi. The irony is sharp: Israel's hearts have been stolen by Absalom, but a Gittite volunteer pledges his life.

**Verse 25-26 — David's prayer of surrender:** These verses are the spiritual center of the entire Absalom narrative. David does not demand that God save him. He does not claim a right to the throne. He places himself entirely in God's hands: "here I am" (*hinneni*) — the same word Abraham used on the way to sacrifice Isaac. David's willingness to accept whatever God decides is the posture of authentic faith under unbearable pressure.

**Verse 30 — the procession of grief:** David ascending the Mount of Olives — weeping, barefoot, head covered — is one of the most visually powerful scenes in the Old Testament. The king who danced before the ark as it entered Jerusalem (ch. 6) now leaves the city as a mourner. His people mirror his posture: covered heads, weeping. It is a funeral procession for a kingdom that is still alive.

*— PNEUMA*
